sentences.l: And she said to-him: O my master, sell of the furnishings of-the-house and its vessels until God the-Exalted arranges, and spend first by first.
sentences.i: She said to him, "My master, sell some of the furnishings of the house and its vessels until God Most High brings some remedy, and spend as you go, a little at a time."

sentences.t: فَبَاعَ إِلَى أَنْ بَاعَ جَمِيعَ مَا فِى الْبَيْتِ وَمَا بَقِيَ عِنْدَهُ شَيُ
sentences.tr: fa-bāʿa ilā an bāʿa jamīʿa mā fī al-bayti wa-mā baqiya ʿindahu shayʾu
sentences.l: And he sold until he sold all that (was) in the house, and nothing remained with him.
sentences.i: So he sold until he had sold everything in the house, and nothing was left to him.
sentences.n: The print gives the last word (شيُ) a single damma on its last letter and no hamza; it is kept as printed and read shayʾ, “anything”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ نَظَرَ إِلَى أَنِيسِ الْجَلِيسِ وَقَالَ لَهَا مَا نَفْعَلُ الْآنَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika naẓara ilā Anīsi al-Jalīsi wa-qāla lahā mā nafʿalu al-āna
sentences.l: And at that he looked to Anīs al-Jalīs and said to-her: What do-we-do now?
sentences.i: Then he looked at Anīs al-Jalīs and said to her, "What shall we do now?"

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي عِنْدِي مِنَ الرَّأْيِ أَنْ تَقُومَ السَّاعَةَ وَتَنْزِلَ بِي إِلَى السُّوقِ وَتَبِيعَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī ʿindī mina al-raʾyi an taqūma al-sāʿata wa-tanzila bī ilā al-sūqi wa-tabīʿanī
sentences.l: And she said to-him: O my master, with-me (is) of opinion that you rise (this) hour and go-down with-me to the market and sell-me.
sentences.i: She said to him, "My master, my counsel is that you rise at once, take me down to the market, and sell me."
sentences.n: عندي من الرأي أن, “I have of opinion that”, is the usual way to offer advice.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ وَالِدَكَ كَانَ اِشْتَرَانِي بِعَشَرَةِ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ فَلَعَلَّ اللَّهَ أَنْ يَفْتَحَ عَلَيْكَ بِقَرِيبٍ مِنْ هَذَا الثَّمَنِ وَإِذَا قَدَّرَ اللَّهُ بِاجْتِمَا عِنَا نَجْتَمِعُ
sentences.tr: wa-anta taʿlamu anna wālidaka kāna ishtarānī bi-ʿasharati ālāfi dīnārin fa-laʿalla Allāha an yaftaḥa ʿalayka bi-qarībin min hādhā al-thamani wa-idhā qaddara Allāhu bi-ijtimāʿinā najtamiʿu
sentences.l: And you know that your father had bought me for ten of-thousands of-dinar; so perhaps God (will) open for-you with a-near of this the-price; and if God decrees by our-gathering, we gather.
sentences.i: You know that your father bought me for ten thousand dinars; perhaps God will open a way for you with a sum near that price. And if God ordains that we be reunited, we shall be.
sentences.n: باجتما عنا is printed as two words and is read bi-ijtimāʿinā, “by our coming together”; it is kept as printed. The sense of the last clause is that if God wills their reunion, they will meet again. آلاف دينار, “thousands of dinar”, is the Classical genitive after the number.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا أَنِيسَ الْجَلِيسِ وَاللَّهِ مَا يَهُونُ عَلَيَّ فِرَاقُكِ سَاعَةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā Anīsa al-Jalīsi wa-Allāhi mā yahūnu ʿalayya firāquki sāʿatan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: And he said to-her: O Anīs al-Jalīs, by-God, your-parting does not become-easy upon me (for) an hour, one.
sentences.i: He said to her, "Anīs al-Jalīs, by God, I cannot bear to part from you for a single hour."

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ يَا سَيِّدِي وَلَا أَنَا لَكِنْ لِلضَّرُورَةِ أَحْكَامٌ كَمَا قَالَ الشَّـــــــــاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu wa-Allāhi yā sayyidī wa-lā anā lākin li-al-ḍarūrati aḥkāmun kamā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And she said to-him: By-God, O my master, nor I; but for-necessity (are) rulings, as said the-poet:
sentences.i: She said to him, "By God, my master, nor can I. But necessity has its own laws, as the poet says:"
sentences.n: ولا أنا, “nor I”, takes up his “I cannot bear it”. للضرورة أحكام, “for necessity there are rulings”, is a proverbial saying, here introducing the verses that follow.

sentences.t:
تُلْجِي الضَّرُورَاتُ فِي الْاُمُورِ اِلَى * سُلُوكِ مَا لَا يَلِيقُ بِالْاَدَبِ
مَا حَامِلٌ نَفْسَهُ عَلَى سَبَبِ * اِلَّا لِاَمْرٍ يَلِيقُ بِالسَّبَبِ
sentences.tr:
tulji al-ḍarūrātu fī al-umūri ilā * sulūki mā lā yalīqu bi-al-adabi
mā ḥāmilun nafsahu ʿalā sababi * illā li-amrin yalīqu bi-al-sababi
sentences.l:
Compel the-necessities, in the-affairs, to * the-following of what not befits with-the-good-manners;
not a-bearer (of) himself upon a-cause * except for a-matter (that) befits with-the-cause.
sentences.i:
Necessity drives men in their affairs * to take paths ill suited to good breeding;
no man loads himself with a pretext * except for a cause that befits it.
sentences.n: Two lines of verse, printed with their vowels; the pointing is kept as printed. The second line says that no one takes up a shift or pretext except for a matter that warrants it, that is, necessity excuses what shame would forbid.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَٰلِكَ نَهَضَ عَلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَأَخَذَ أَنِيسَ الْجَلِيسِ وَدُمُوعُهُ تَسِيلُ عَلَى خَدِّهِ كَالْمَطَرِ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ بِلِسَانِ الْحَالِ وَقَالَ شِعْـــــــــرًا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika nahaḍa ʿalā qadamayhi wa-akhadha Anīsa al-Jalīsi wa-dumūʿuhu tasīlu ʿalā khaddihi ka-al-maṭari thumma anshada bi-lisāni al-ḥāli wa-qāla shiʿran
sentences.l: And at that, he rose on his two feet, and took Anīs al-Jalīs, while his tears flowed on his cheek like the rain; then he recited with the tongue of the state, and said poetry:
sentences.i: Thereupon he rose to his feet and took Anīs al-Jalīs with him, while the tears ran down his cheek like rain; then he spoke in the very voice of his plight, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: فعند ذلك is “at that”, hence “thereupon”, the narrator’s usual way of moving the story on. بلسان الحال (“with the tongue of the state”) means speaking as one’s condition itself would speak, so the poem is his situation put into words. The print draws out شعرا with a row of tatweel (stretching strokes), which only marks that verse follows; it is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
قِفُوا زَوِّدُونِي نَظْرَةً قَبْلَ بَيْنِكُمْ * اُعَلِّلُ قَلْبًا كَادَ بِالْبَيْنِ يَتْلَفُ
فَإِنْ كُنْتُمُو تَلْقَوْنَ فِي ذَاكَ كُلْفَةً * دَعُونِي أَمُتْ وَجْدًا وَلَا تَتَكَلَّفُ
sentences.tr:
qifū zawwidūnī naẓratan qabla baynikum * uʿallilu qalban kāda bi-al-bayni yatlafu
fa-in kuntumū talqawna fī dhāka kulfatan * daʿūnī amut wajdan wa-lā tatakallafu
sentences.l: Stop! Provision me with a glance before your parting; I console a heart that almost perished at the parting. / And if you find in that any trouble — leave me, I shall die of passion, and do not trouble-yourself.
sentences.i: Halt, and spare me one last glance before you part; I would beguile a heart that was near to perishing at your leaving. But if you find that too great a burden, then leave me to die of love, and trouble yourselves no further.
sentences.n: The print points this poem itself, and the pointing is copied unchanged. كنتمو has the poetic long ū added to the 2 m. pl. ending -tum. ولا تتكلف is singular in form while the verse addresses a company; it is kept as printed (a plural jussive would end in -ū, which the rhyme in -fu does not allow). أعلل shows the print’s damma on a bare alif, with no hamza written.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَضَى وَنَزَلَ بِهَا إِلَى السُّوقِ وَسَلَّمَهَا لِلدَّلَّالِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا حَاجُّ حَسَنُ اعْرِفْ قَدْرَ مَا تُنَادِى عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma maḍā wa-nazala bihā ilā al-sūqi wa-sallamahā li-al-dallāli wa-qāla lahu yā ḥājju Ḥasanu iʿrif qadra mā tunādī ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then he went off, and went down with her to the market, and handed-her-over to-the-broker, and said to-him: O pilgrim Ḥasan, know the worth of what you cry upon.
sentences.i: Then he went down with her to the market, handed her over to the broker, and said to him, “Ḥājj Ḥasan, know her worth before you cry her for sale.”
sentences.n: حاج حسن is the broker’s name with his title of one who has made the pilgrimage, “Ḥājj Ḥasan”. نادى على (“to call upon”) is the auctioneer’s verb for crying a lot for sale; the print spells the final -ī of تنادي with ى, a common Middle Arabic spelling, and it is vocalised as the ordinary 2 m. sing. imperfect.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الدَّلَّالُ يَا سَيِّدِي نُورَالدِّينِ الْأَصُولُ مَحْفُوظَةٌ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ هَٰذِهِ مَا هِيَ أَنِيسُ الْجَلِيسِ الَّتِي كَانَتِ اشْتَرَاهَا وَالِدُكَ مِنِّي بِعَشَرَةِ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ قَالَ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-dallālu yā sayyidī Nūra al-Dīni al-uṣūlu maḥfūẓatun thumma qāla lahu hādhihi mā hiya Anīsu al-Jalīsi allatī kānati ishtarāhā wālidukā minnī bi-ʿashrati ālāfi dīnārin qāla naʿam
sentences.l: So said the broker: O my master Nūr al-Dīn, the principles are kept. Then he said to him: This one — is she not Anīs al-Jalīs, who had been bought by your father from me for ten thousands of dinars? He said: Yes.
sentences.i: The broker said, “My lord Nūr al-Dīn, the proprieties are kept.” Then he said to him, “Is this not Anīs al-Jalīs, whom your father bought from me for ten thousand dinars?” “Yes,” said Nūr al-Dīn.
sentences.n: الأصول محفوظة (“the principles are kept”) is the broker’s courteous way of saying that he knows the proper form of business and will observe it. هذه ما هي is a question put by negation, “this one, is she not…?”; ما is not read here as “what”. كانت اشتراها is a pluperfect, “had bought her”, with the auxiliary agreeing with التي. نورالدين is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَٰلِكَ طَلَعَ الدَّلَّالُ إِلَى التُّجَّارِ فَوَجَدَ هُمْ مَا اجْتَمَعُوا كُلُّهُمْ فَصَبَرَ حَتَّى اجْتَمَعَ سَائِرُ التُّجَّارِ وَاحْتَبَكَ السُّوقُ بِسَائِرِ أَجْنَاسِ الْجَوَارِي مِنْ تُرْكِيَّةٍ وَأَفْرَنْجِيَّةٍ وَشَرْكَسِيَّةٍ وَحَبَشِيَّةٍ وَنُوبِيَّةٍ وَتَكْرُورِيَّةٍ وَرُومِيَّةٍ وَتَتَرِيَّةٍ وَجُرْجِيَّةٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṭalaʿa al-dallālu ilā al-tujjāri fa-wajada hum mā ijtamaʿū kulluhum fa-ṣabara ḥattā ijtamaʿa sāʾiru al-tujjāri wa-iḥtabaka al-sūqu bi-sāʾiri ajnāsi al-jawārī min turkiyyatin wa-afranjiyyatin wa-sharkasiyyatin wa-ḥabashiyyatin wa-nūbiyyatin wa-takrūriyyatin wa-rūmiyyatin wa-tatariyyatin wa-jurjiyyatin wa-ghayri dhālika
sentences.l: And at that, the broker went up to the merchants and found them — not (yet) had they gathered, all-of-them — so he was patient until gathered the whole-of the merchants, and the market became densely-packed with the whole-of the kinds of the slave-girls: from a Turkish and a Frankish and a Circassian and an Abyssinian and a Nubian and a Takrūrī and a Greek and a Tatar and a Georgian, and other-than that.
sentences.i: Thereupon the broker went up to the merchants and found that they had not yet all gathered; so he waited until every merchant had come and the market was packed with slave-girls of every kind: Turkish, Frankish, Circassian, Abyssinian, Nubian, Takrūrī, Greek, Tatar, Georgian, and others besides.
sentences.n: فوجد هم is printed with a space before the pronoun, but it is one word, “and he found them”. سائر here means “all, the whole of”, not “the rest”. The list of slave-girls gives each nationality as a feminine adjective in the genitive after من; رومية is Rūmī, a woman from the lands of Byzantium and Greece, and تكرورية is from Takrūr in West Africa. جرجية is read as “Georgian”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَا لِلدَّلَّالِ إِلَى السُّوقِ قَدِ احْتَبَكَ تَقَدَّمَ وَنَهَضَ قَائِمًا وَقَالَ يَا تُجَّارِيَا أَرْبَابَ الْأَ مْوَالِ مَا كُلُّ مُدَوَّرَةٍ جَوْزَةٌ وَلَا كُلُّ مُسْتَطِيلَةٍ مَوْزَةٌ وَلَا كُلُّ حَمْرَاءَ لَحْمَةٌ وَلَا كُلُّ بَيْضَاءَ شَحْمَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓarā li-al-dallāli ilā al-sūqi qadi iḥtabaka taqaddama wa-nahaḍa qāʾiman wa-qāla yā tujjārīyā arbāba al-a mwāli mā kullu mudawwaratin jawzatun wa-lā kullu mustaṭīlatin mawzatun wa-lā kullu ḥamrāʾa laḥmatun wa-lā kullu bayḍāʾa shaḥmatun
sentences.l: And when he looked, the broker, at the market, it having become packed, he stepped forward and rose standing, and said: O my merchants, masters of the wealth, not every round (thing) is a nut, nor every oblong (thing) a banana, nor every red (thing) flesh, nor every white (thing) fat.
sentences.i: When the broker saw that the market was packed, he stepped forward, stood up, and said, “O my merchants, masters of wealth, not every round thing is a nut, nor every long thing a banana, nor every red thing meat, nor every white thing fat.”
sentences.n: The print has نظرا للدلال, which does not parse as it stands; it looks like a slip for نظر الدلال, “the broker looked”, and is vocalised with the letters as printed (نَظَرَا لِلدَّلَّالِ) and translated by the evident sense. يا تجاريا is obscure; it is read as “O my merchants”, with a final ā of address. الا موال is the single word الأموال (“the wealth”) printed with a space inside it, so it is split here, with the hamza and the sukūn of the mīm shown on the two halves. The last four clauses are a proverbial warning that appearances deceive.

sentences.t: يَا تُجَّارُ مَعِي هَٰذِهِ الدُّرَّةُ الْيَتِيمَةُ الَّتِي مَا لَهَا قِيمَةٌ كَمْ أُنَادِي عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: yā tujjāru maʿī hādhihi al-durratu al-yatīmatu allatī mā lahā qīmatun kam unādī ʿalayhā
sentences.l: O merchants, with me (is) this pearl, the orphan, which not for-her (is) any price: how much shall I cry upon her?
sentences.i: Merchants, I have here this matchless pearl, which has no price. At what shall I cry her?
sentences.n: الدرة اليتيمة, “the orphan pearl”, is a pearl without a fellow, so “matchless”; the praise is the broker’s patter for the slave-girl. ما لها قيمة (“she has no price”) is the usual compliment that a thing is beyond value. كم أنادي عليها asks at what sum he shall open the bidding.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاحِدٌ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ نَادِ بِأَرْبَعَةِ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ وَخَمْسِمِائَةٍ فَفَتَحَ بَابَهَا الْمُنَادِي أَرْبَعَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ وَخَمْسِمِائَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wāḥidun mina al-tujjāri nādi bi-arbaʿati ālāfi dīnārin wa-khamsimiʾatin fa-fataḥa bābahā al-munādī arbaʿata ālāfi dīnārin wa-khamsimiʾatin
sentences.l: So said one from the merchants: Cry at four of-thousands of-dinar and five-hundred. And the crier opened her door (at) four of-thousands of-dinar and five-hundred.
sentences.i: One of the merchants said, “Open the bidding at four thousand five hundred dinars.” And the crier opened the bidding on her at four thousand five hundred dinars.
sentences.n: فتح بابها (“he opened her door”) is the idiom for starting the bidding on a lot. The numeral is a stock one: the counted noun dīnār stands in the genitive after ālāf, and the hundreds are joined on with و. In the print خمسمائة has the precomposed ئ, which is kept.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ يَقُولُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَإِذَا بِالْوَزِيرِ الْمُعِينِ اِبْنِ سَاوَى فِى السُّوقِ عَابِرٌ فَنَظَرَ إِلَى نُورِ الدِّينِ عَلِيٍّ وَاقِفًا فِي طَرَفِ السُّوقِ فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa yaqūlu hādhā al-kalāma wa-idhā bi-al-wazīri al-Muʿīni ibni Sāwā fī al-sūqi ʿābirun fa-naẓara ilā Nūri al-Dīni ʿAliyyin wāqifan fī ṭarafi al-sūqi fa-qāla fī nafsihi
sentences.l: And he saying this the speech, and behold, with-the-vizier, al-Muʿīn, son-of Sāwī, in the market (was) passing; so he looked at Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī standing at the edge of the market, and said in his self:
sentences.i: While he was saying this, behold, the vizier al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī was passing through the market; and he looked and saw Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī standing at the edge of the market, and said to himself:
sentences.n: The scene turns to the rival vizier, who happens by. After وَإِذَا, بِالْوَزِيرِ only marks what appears (“and behold, the vizier”), and the participle عَابِرٌ says what he was doing. The print writes فى (with dotless ى) in one place and في in another; both are kept as printed.

sentences.t: مَابَالُ اِبْنِ خَاقَانَ وَاقِفًا هَهُنَا أَبَقِيَ مَعَ هَذَا الْعِلْقِ شَيْ يَشْتَرِي بِهِ الْجَوَارِيَ
sentences.tr: mā bālu ibni Khāqāna wāqifan hahunā abaqiya maʿa hādhā al-ʿilqi shay yashtarī bihi al-jawāriya
sentences.l: What (is) the concern of the son-of Khāqān, standing here? Has there remained with this ʿilq a thing (that) he buys with it the slave-girls?
sentences.i: What ails the son of Khāqān, that he stands here? Has this fellow anything left to buy slave-girls with?
sentences.n: The print has العلق, vocalised here as الْعِلْقِ, ʿilq, which in Lane is a precious thing; said of a man it can only be contemptuous (“this fellow”, as if “this item”). The word is obscure and the reading is a guess; the sense of the vizier’s sneer is clear. شَيْ is the print’s شي without the hamza of شيء, the usual Middle Arabic spelling; the accusative الْجَوَارِيَ keeps the full ending that Classical would drop.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ بِعَيْنِهِ فَسَمِعَ الْمُنَادِيَ وَهُوَ وَاقِفٌ يُنَادِي فِى السُّوقِ وَالتُّجَّارُ حَوْلَهُ فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَا أَظُنُّهُ إِلَّا أَفْلَسَ وَنَزَلَ بِالْجَارِيَةِ أَنِيسِ الْجَلِيسِ لِيَبِيعَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara bi-ʿaynihi fa-samiʿa al-munādiya wa-huwa wāqifun yunādī fī al-sūqi wa-al-tujjāru ḥawlahu fa-qāla al-wazīru fī nafsihi mā aẓunnuhu illā aflasa wa-nazala bi-al-jāriyati Anīsi al-Jalīsi li-yabīʿahā
sentences.l: Then he looked with his eye, and heard the crier, he standing calling in the market, and the merchants around him; and the vizier said in his self: I do not think him (to be) other-than that he has gone-bankrupt, and has come-down with the slave-girl Anīs al-Jalīs in-order-that he sell her.
sentences.i: Then he looked about and heard the crier standing and crying in the market, with the merchants gathered round him; and the vizier said to himself, "I can only think he has gone bankrupt and brought down the slave-girl Anīs al-Jalīs to sell her."
sentences.n: The merchants’ clause وَالتُّجَّارُ حَوْلَهُ is a circumstantial “with the merchants round him”. The vizier’s thought is a negative-plus-illā construction, “I think nothing of him except that he has gone bankrupt”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ يَا بَرْدَهَا عَلَى قَلْبِي ثُمَّ دَعَا الْمُنَادِيَ فَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ فَقَالَ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي تُنَادِي عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla fī nafsihi yā bardahā ʿalā qalbī thumma daʿā al-munādiya fa-aqbala ʿalayhi wa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi fa-qāla innī urīdu hādhihi al-jāriyata allatī tunādī ʿalayhā
sentences.l: Then he said in his self: O its-coolness upon my heart! Then he called the crier, and he came-forward upon him, and kissed the earth between his two hands; and he said: Indeed I want this slave-girl which you call over.
sentences.i: Then he said to himself, "How cool it will lie upon my heart!" and called the crier, who came up to him and kissed the ground before him. And the vizier said, "I want this slave-girl whom you are crying."
sentences.n: يَا بَرْدَهَا عَلَى قَلْبِي is an exclamation of satisfaction: cool is what soothes, so “how cool it will be upon my heart” means the vizier relishes the thought of taking the girl from his enemy’s son. The print marks the vowels of بَرْدَها; they are kept as printed. نَادَى عَلَى is the auctioneer’s verb: to cry a lot for sale.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَمْكَنَهُ الْمُخَالَفَةُ فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي بِسْمِ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ الْجَارِيَةَ وَأَعْرَضَهَا عَلَيْهِ فَأَعْجَبَتْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā amkanahu al-mukhālafatu fa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī bismi Allāhi thumma taqaddama al-jāriyata wa-aʿraḍahā ʿalayhi fa-aʿjabathu
sentences.l: So not was-possible for him the opposing; and he said to him: O my lord, in-the-name-of God! Then he went-before the slave-girl, and presented her upon him, and she pleased him.
sentences.i: The crier could not refuse him, and said, "In God’s name, my lord!" Then he brought the girl forward and showed her to him, and she pleased him.
sentences.n: Here taqaddama takes a direct object (“advance the girl”), and أَعْرَضَهَا is the fourth form for the ordinary ʿaraḍahā, “presented her”; both are Middle Arabic looseness that the sense makes plain. بِسْمِ اللَّهِ is the courteous “by all means”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا حَسَنُ كَمْ مَعَكَ فِي هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةِ فَقَالَ لَهُ أَرْبَعَةُ آلَافٍ وَخَمْسُمِائَةِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā Ḥasanu kam maʿaka fī hādhihi al-jāriyati fa-qāla lahu arbaʿatu ālāfin wa-khamsumiʾati dīnārin
sentences.l: So he said to him: O Ḥasan, how-much (is) with you in this slave-girl? He said to him: Four thousands and five-hundred of dinars.
sentences.i: Then he said, "Ḥasan, how much have you for this girl?" and the crier answered, "Four thousand five hundred dinars."
sentences.n: The crier’s name is Ḥasan. “How much is with you in her” asks for the standing bid.

sentences.t: فُتِحَ الْبَابُ قَالَ الْمُعِينُ عَلَيَّ أَرْبَعَةُ آلَافٍ وَخَمْسُمِائَةِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: futiḥa al-bābu qāla al-Muʿīnu ʿalayya arbaʿatu ālāfin wa-khamsumiʾati dīnārin
sentences.l: Opened (was) the door. The Muʿīn said: Upon me (be) four thousands and five-hundred of dinars.
sentences.i: "The bidding is open," said al-Muʿīn, "and four thousand five hundred dinars are on me."
sentences.n: “The door is opened” is the auction’s phrase for the opening bid; the print marks the damma of فُتح and the shadda of عليّ, and both are kept. عَلَيَّ “upon me” is how a bidder takes a sum on himself.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التُّجَّارُ ذَلِكَ مَا نَدَرَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ أَنْ يُزَوِّدَ دِرْهَمًا بَلْ تَأَخَّرُوا لِمَا يَعْلَمُونَ مِنْ ظُلْمِ الْوَزِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tujjāru dhālika mā nadara wāḥidun minhum an yuzawwida dirhaman bal taʾakhkharū li-mā yaʿlamūna min ẓulmi al-wazīri
sentences.l: So when the merchants heard that, not did one of them stand-out to add a dirham; rather they held-back, because-of what they know from the wrongdoing of the vizier.
sentences.i: When the merchants heard that, not one of them ventured to bid so much as a dirham more; they held back, for they knew the vizier’s tyranny.
sentences.n: يُزَوِّدَ is read as zawwada, “add”; the form is not found in the dictionaries for this sense, and the reading follows the context (a bid raised by a dirham). نَدَرَ أَنْ is “to venture to”, literally “to stand out so as to”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ الْمُعِينُ بْنُ سَاوَى إِلَى الدَّلَّالِ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَيْشْ وُقُوفُكَ رُحْ وَشَاوِرْ عَلَيَّ بِأَرْبَعَةِ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ وَلَكَ خَمْسُمِائَةِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara al-Muʿīnu ibnu Sāwā ilā al-dallāli wa-qāla lahu ayš wuqūfuka ruḥ wa-shāwir ʿalayya bi-arbaʿati ālāfi dīnārin wa-laka khamsumiʾatu dīnārin
sentences.l: Then al-Muʿīn son-of Sāwī looked at the crier, and said to him: What (is) your standing? Go and bid upon me with four thousands of dinars, and to-you (are) five-hundred dinars.
sentences.i: Then al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī looked at the crier and said, "Why do you stand there? Go and cry four thousand dinars on my account, and five hundred shall be yours."
sentences.n: أَيْشْ is the colloquial “what?” (for أَيُّ شَيْءٍ); رُحْ is the colloquial imperative of رَاحَ “go”; شَاوِرْ عَلَى is “bid for”, a use of shāwara particular to the market. The extra five hundred is the crier’s reward for bidding on the vizier’s behalf.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ الدَّلَّالُ إِلَي نُورِ الدِّينِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي رَاحَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ عَلَيْكَ بِلَا شَيْ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-dallālu ilā Nūri al-Dīni wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī rāḥati al-jāriyatu ʿalayka bi-lā shay
sentences.l: So the crier advanced to Nūr al-Dīn, and said to him: O my lord, gone has the slave-girl upon you, with-no thing.
sentences.i: So the crier went up to Nūr al-Dīn and said, "My lord, the girl is lost to you, and you have nothing for her."
sentences.n: The print writes إلي with a dotted ي; it is read as إِلَى. رَاحَتْ عَلَيْكَ is the idiom for “went from you, was lost to you”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ وَكَيْفَ قَالَ لَهُ نَحْنُ فَتَحْنَا بَا بَهَا أَرْبَعَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ وَخَمْسُمِائَهْ فَجَاءَ هَذَا الظَّالِمُ الْمُعِينُ بْنُ سَاوَى وَعَبَرَ السُّوقَ فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ أَعْجَبَتْهُ وَقَالَ لِي شَاوِرْ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ آلَافٍ وَلَكَ خَمْسُمِائَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu wa-kayfa qāla lahu naḥnu fataḥnā bā bahā arbaʿata ālāfi dīnārin wa-khamsumiʾah fa-jāʾa hādhā al-ẓālimu al-Muʿīnu ibnu Sāwā wa-ʿabara al-sūqa fa-lammā naẓara ilā al-jāriyati aʿjabathu wa-qāla lī shāwir ʿalā arbaʿati ālāfin wa-laka khamsumiʾatin
sentences.l: So he said to him: And how? He said to him: We, we opened her door (at) four thousands of dinars and five-hundred; then came this wrongdoer, al-Muʿīn son-of Sāwī, and crossed the market; and when he looked at the slave-girl she pleased him, and he said to me: Bid upon four thousands, and to-you five-hundred.
sentences.i: "How so?" said Nūr al-Dīn. And the crier said, "We opened the bidding at four thousand five hundred dinars; then this tyrant al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī came by, crossing the market, and when he saw the girl she took his fancy, and he said to me, 'Cry four thousand, and five hundred shall be yours.'"
sentences.n: The print divides the word بابها (“her door”) as با بها across the line; it is kept as two words and each is vocalised as part of bābahā. “Opening her door” is the opening of the bidding. The final وخمسمائه is printed with ه for ة and is read as the pausal form -ah.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَظُنُّهُ إِلَّا عَرَفَ أَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ لَكَ وَإِنْ كَانَ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ يُعْطِيكَ ثَمَنَهَا يَكُونُ مَلِيحًا
sentences.tr: wa-mā aẓunnuhu illā ʿarafa anna al-jāriyata laka wa-in kāna fī hādhihi al-sāʿati yuʿṭīka thamanahā yakūnu malīḥan
sentences.l: And not I-think-him other-than that he knew that the slave-girl (is) yours; and if (it be) that in this hour he gives you her price, it will be fine.
sentences.i: I can only think he knew the girl was yours. If he were to pay you her price this very hour, well and good.
sentences.n: وَإِنْ كَانَ يُعْطِيكَ is a loose conditional, with the verb يُعْطِي following كَانَ directly and the result clause يَكُونُ مَلِيحًا unmarked by فَـ; مَلِيحًا is colloquial for “fine, good”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَعْرِفُ مِنْ ظُلْمِهِ أَنَّهُ يَكْتُبُ لَكَ وَرَقَةً حَوَالَةً عَلَى بَعْضِ عُمَّالِهِ ثُمَّ يُرْسِلُ خَلْفَكَ أَحَدًا وَيَقُولُ لَهُمْ لَا تُعْطُوهُ شَيْأً
sentences.tr: wa-anā aʿrifu min ẓulmihi annahu yaktubu laka waraqatan ḥawālatan ʿalā baʿḍi ʿummālihi thumma yursilu khalfaka aḥadan wa-yaqūlu lahum lā tuʿṭūhu shayʾan
sentences.l: And I, I know from his wrongdoing that he writes for you a paper, a draft upon some of his agents, then sends behind you someone, and says to them: Do not give him anything.
sentences.i: I know his tyranny: he will write you a note, a draft on one of his agents, and then send someone after you to say to them, "Give him nothing."
sentences.n: حَوَالَةً is a draft or order of payment, in apposition to وَرَقَةً. The man sent after Nūr al-Dīn is singular (أَحَدًا) but the agents he instructs are plural (لَهُمْ), as printed.

sentences.t: فَكُلَّمَا رُحْتَ تُطَالِبُهُمْ يَقُولُونَ السَّاعَةَ نُعْطِيكَ وَيَعْمَلُونَ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ مَعَكَ يَوْمًا بَعْدَ يَوْمٍ وَأَنْتَ عَزِيرُ النَّفْسِ وَبَعْدَ أَنْ يَضِجُّوا مِنْ طَلَبِكَ لَهُمْ يَقُولُونَ أَرِنَا الْوَرَقَةَ فَإِذَا أَخَذُوا الْوَرَقَةَ مِنْكَ قَطَعُوهَا وَيَرُوحُ مِنْكَ ثَمَنُ الْجَارِيَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-kullamā ruḥta tuṭālibuhum yaqūlūna al-sāʿata nuʿṭīka wa-yaʿmalūna hādhā al-amra maʿaka yawman baʿda yawmin wa-anta ʿazīru al-nafsi wa-baʿda an yaḍijjū min ṭalabika lahum yaqūlūna arinā al-waraqata fa-idhā akhadhū al-waraqata minka qaṭaʿūhā wa-yarūḥu minka thamanu al-jāriyati
sentences.l: So whenever you went (to) demand of them, they say: This hour we give you! And they do this matter with you, day after day, and you (are) ʿazīr of the self; and after they are fed-up with your asking from them, they say: Show us the paper! And when they take the paper from you they tear it, and goes from you the price of the slave-girl.
sentences.i: Every time you go to press them, they will say, "We shall pay you at once," and so they will put you off day after day, while you stand on your dignity; and when they are weary of your dunning they will say, "Show us the paper," and the moment they have it from you they will tear it up, and the price of the girl is gone from you.
sentences.n: رُحْتَ تُطَالِبُهُمْ, “you went, you demand of them”, uses رَاحَ as a helping verb, “you go and demand”. The print has عزير النفس; ʿazīz al-nafs, “proud, self-respecting”, would be the expected word, so عزير looks like a slip for عزيز, but it is vocalised as printed and the sense (a man too proud to keep pestering) is kept. السَّاعَةَ is “at once, straight away”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ نُورُ الدِّينِ عَلِيٌّ مِنَ الدَّلَّالِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ هَذَا الْعَمَلُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Nūru al-Dīni ʿAliyyun mina al-dallāli hādhā al-kalāma naẓara ilayhi wa-qāla lahu kayfa yakūnu hādhā al-ʿamalu
sentences.l: So when Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī heard from the crier this speech, he looked at him and said to him: How will this doing be?
sentences.i: When Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī heard these words from the crier, he looked at him and said, "What, then, is to be done?"

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَنَا أُشَوِّرُ عَلَيْكَ بِمَشُورَةٍ فَإِنْ قَبِلْتَ مِنِّي كَانَ لَكَ الْحَظُّ الْأَوْفَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu anā ushawwiru ʿalayka bi-mashūratin fa-in qabilta minnī kāna laka al-ḥaẓẓu al-awfaru
sentences.l: So he said to him: I, I counsel upon you with a counsel; and if you accept from me, there will be for you the fortune, the ampler.
sentences.i: He said, "I shall give you a piece of counsel, and if you take it from me, the best of fortune will be yours."
sentences.n: أُشَوِّرُ is read as the second-form of شَارَ “advise”, the sense of أَشَارَ عَلَى, with the noun مَشُورَةٌ “counsel” as its cognate object; الْأَوْفَرُ is the elative, “the fullest, richest”.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَمَا هِيَ قَالَ تَجِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةَ إِلَى عِنْدِي وَأَنَا وَاقِفٌ وَسَطَ السُّوقِ وَتَأْخُذُ الْجَارِيَةَ مِنْ يَدِي وَتَلْطُمُهَا وَتَقُولُ لَهَا يَاكُورَةُ فَدَيْتُ يَمِينِي الَّذِي حَلَفْتُهُ وَنَزَلْتُ بِكِ السُّوقَ حَيْثُ حَلَفْتُ عَلَيْكِ أَنَّهُ لَابُدَّ مِنْ إِخْرَاجِكِ إِلَى السُّوقِ وَمُنَادَاةِ الدَّلَّالِ عَلَيْكِ
sentences.tr: qāla wa-mā hiya qāla tajī hādhihi al-sāʿata ilā ʿindī wa-anā wāqifun wasaṭa al-sūqi wa-taʾkhudhu al-jāriyata min yadī wa-talṭumuhā wa-taqūlu lahā yā kūratu fadaytu yamīnī alladhī ḥalaftuhu wa-nazaltu bi-ki al-sūqa ḥaythu ḥalaftu ʿalayki annahu lā budda min ikhrājiki ilā al-sūqi wa-munādāti al-dallāli ʿalayki
sentences.l: He said: And what is it? He said: You come this hour to at-me, and I standing the middle of the market, and you take the slave-girl from my hand, and slap her, and say to her: O kūra! I have redeemed my oath which I swore it, and I brought-you-down to the market, since I swore upon you that (there is) no avoiding from your bringing-out to the market, and the crying-out of the crier upon you.
sentences.i: "And what is that?" said he. "That you come to me at this very hour, while I am standing in the middle of the market, and take the girl from my hand and slap her, and say to her: 'You wretch! I have made good the oath I swore: I took you down to the market because I swore to you that you must be brought out to the market and cried by the crier.'"
sentences.n: The advice is given as a run of present-tense verbs (“you come, and take, and slap, and say”) with no subjunctive after the first, which is how the dialect gives instructions. كُورَة is obscure: it may be the Persian-derived کور “blind” used as an insult, or the Arabic kūra “lump, ball”; it is taken here as an abusive vocative, “wretch”, and the print writes it joined to يا. فَدَيْتُ يَمِينِي is “I have redeemed (made good) my oath”.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ فَعَلْتَ ذَلِكَ رُبَّمَا تَنْطَلِقُ عَلَيْهِ الْحِيلَةُ وَعَلَى النَّاسِ وَيَعْتَقِدُونَ أَنَّكَ مَا نَزَلْتَ بِهَا إِلَى السُّوقِ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِ إِبْرَارِ الْيَمِينِ
sentences.tr: fa-in faʿalta dhālika rubbamā tanṭaliqu ʿalayhi al-ḥīlatu wa-ʿalā al-nāsi wa-yaʿtaqidūna annaka mā nazalta bihā ilā al-sūqi illā li-ajli ibrāri al-yamīni
sentences.l: So if you do that, perhaps the trick will go-through upon him and upon the people, and they will believe that you did not bring-her-down to the market except for the sake of the fulfilling of the oath.
sentences.i: If you do this, the trick may well pass upon him and upon the people, and they will believe that you took her down to the market only to keep your oath.
sentences.n: انْطَلَقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْحِيلَةُ is “the trick went through on him, he was taken in”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ هَذَا هُوَ الصَّوَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla hādhā huwa al-ṣawābu
sentences.l: So he said: This, it (is) the right.
sentences.i: "That is the right course," he said.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الدَّلَّالَ فَارَقَهُ وَجَاءَ وَسَطَ السُّوقِ وَمَسَكَ يَدَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَأَشَارَ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ الْمُعِينِ بْنِ سَاوَى وَقَالَ يَامَوْلَاىَ هَذَا مَا لِكُهَا قَدْ أَقْبَلَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-dallāla fāraqahu wa-jāʾa wasaṭa al-sūqi wa-masaka yada al-jāriyati wa-ashāra ilā al-wazīri al-Muʿīni ibni Sāwā wa-qāla yā mawlāya hādhā mā likuhā qad aqbala
sentences.l: Then indeed the crier left him, and came (to) the middle of the market, and grasped the hand of the slave-girl, and pointed to the vizier, al-Muʿīn son-of Sāwī, and said: O my master, this (is) her owner, he has come.
sentences.i: Then the crier left him, came into the middle of the market, took the girl by the hand and pointed to the vizier al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī, saying, "My lord, here is her owner, who has just arrived."
sentences.n: The print splits مالكها (“her owner”) as ما لكها; it is kept as two words and read mālikuhā. The vizier is addressed as يَا مَوْلَايَ, “my lord”, spelled with final ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَاءَ نُورُ الدِّينِ إِلَى الدَّلَّالِ وَنَزَعَ الْجَارِيَةَ مِنْ يَدِهِ وَلَكَمَهَا وَقَالَ لَهَا وَيْلَكِ يَاكُورَةُ نَزَلْتُ بِكِ السُّوقَ لِأَجْلِ فِدَاءِ يَمِينِي رُوحِي إِلَى الْبَيْتِ وَلَا تَعُودِي تُخَالِفِينِي وَيْلَكِ أَنَا مُحْتَاجٌ إِلَى ثَمَنِكِ
sentences.tr: thumma jāʾa Nūru al-Dīni ilā al-dallāli wa-nazaʿa al-jāriyata min yadihi wa-lakamahā wa-qāla lahā waylaki yā kūratu nazaltu bi-ki al-sūqa li-ajli fidāʾi yamīnī rūḥī ilā al-bayti wa-lā taʿūdī tukhālifīnī waylaki anā muḥtājun ilā thamaniki
sentences.l: Then Nūr al-Dīn came to the crier, and snatched the slave-girl from his hand, and struck her with the fist, and said to her: Woe-to-you, O kūra! I brought-you-down to the market for the sake of the redeeming of my oath. Go to the house, and do not return (to) oppose me. Woe-to-you! I (am) in-need of your price
sentences.i: Then Nūr al-Dīn came to the crier, snatched the girl from his hand and struck her, and said, "Curse you, wretch! I brought you to the market only to make good my oath. Go home, and never defy me again. Curse you! Am I in need of your price
sentences.n: وَيْلَكِ is “woe to you”, a curse flung at her in play. The sentence runs on into the next unit: the question of whether he needs her price is answered there. لَا تَعُودِي تُخَالِفِينِي, “do not return, you oppose me”, again leaves the second verb in the plain indicative, as Middle Arabic does.

sentences.t: حَتَّى أَبِيعَكِ أَنَا لَوْ بِعْتُ أَثَاثَ الْبَيْتِ جَاءَ قَدْرَ ثَمَنِكِ مِرَارًا عَدِيدَةً
sentences.tr: ḥattā abīʿaki anā law biʿtu athātha al-bayti jāʾa qadra thamaniki mirāran ʿadīdatan
sentences.l: until I sell you? I — if I sold the furnishings of the house, it would come (to) the measure of your price, times many.
sentences.i: that I should sell you? If I sold the furnishings of the house, they would fetch your price many times over."
sentences.n: This unit finishes the sentence begun in the one before: “am I in need of your price, until (so that) I should sell you?” is Nūr al-Dīn’s feigned scorn, spoken so the watching vizier will believe it. Notice that جَاءَ is followed by an accusative, جَاءَ قَدْرَ ثَمَنِكِ, “it came to the measure of your price”, with the verb left in the singular for the whole household of goods.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ الْمُعِينُ ابْنُ سَاوِى إِلَى نُورِ الدِّينِ قَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ هَلْ بَقِيَ عِنْدَكَ شَيْءٌ يُبَاعُ أَوْ يُشْتَرَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara al-Muʿīnu ibnu Sāwī ilā Nūr al-Dīn qāla lahu waylaka hal baqiya ʿindaka shayʾun yubāʿu aw yushtarā
sentences.l: And when al-Muʿīn, son of Sāwī, looked at Nūr al-Dīn, he said to him: Woe-to-you, has there remained with you a thing that is sold or is bought?
sentences.i: When al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī caught sight of Nūr al-Dīn, he said to him, "Woe to you! Have you anything left that can be bought or sold?"
sentences.n: His taunt is aimed at the slave-girl whom Nūr al-Dīn has already sold; the print gives ساوى with final ى, vocalised here as Sāwī, as in the earlier nights.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمُعِينَ بْنَ سَاوِى أَرَادَأَنْ يَبْطِشَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-Muʿīna bna Sāwī arāda an yabṭisha bihi
sentences.l: Then indeed al-Muʿīn, son of Sāwī, wanted that he-lay-violent-hold with-him.
sentences.i: Then al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī made to lay violent hands on him.
sentences.n: The print runs ارادان together as one word; it is read as أَرَادَ أَنْ, “he wanted to”, and vocalised in one piece. يبطش به, “to seize him violently”, takes its object with بِـ.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَٰلِكَ نَظَرَ التُّجَّارُ إِلَى نُورِ الدِّينِ وَكَانُوا كُلُّهُمْ يُحِبُّونَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُمْ هَا أَنَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيكُمْ وَقَدْ عَرَفْتُمْ ظُلْمَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika naẓara al-tujjāru ilā Nūr al-Dīn wa-kānū kulluhum yuḥibbūnahu fa-qāla lahum hā anā bayna aydīkum wa-qad ʿaraftum ẓulmahu
sentences.l: And at that, the merchants looked at Nūr al-Dīn, and they were, all of them, loving him; and he said to them: Lo, I (am) between your hands, and you have known his wrong-doing.
sentences.i: At that, the merchants turned their eyes to Nūr al-Dīn, for all of them loved him, and he said to them, "Here I stand before you, and you know well his tyranny."
sentences.n: The speaker of هَا أَنَا is Nūr al-Dīn. بَيْنَ أَيْدِيكُمْ, “between your hands”, is the idiom for “in front of you, at your disposal”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ وَاللَّهِ لَوْلَا أَنْتُمْ لَقَتَلْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru wa-Allāhi law-lā antum la-qataltuhu
sentences.l: And the vizier said: By God, were-it-not for you, I would have killed him.
sentences.i: The vizier said, "By God, were it not for you, I would have killed him!"
sentences.n: After لَوْلَا the pronoun أَنْتُمْ stands in the nominative, and the result clause takes لَـ: “were it not for you, I would have killed him”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَشَارُ وَاكُلُّهُمْ إِلَي نُورِ الدِّينِ بِعَيْنِ الْإِشَارَةِ افْتَصِلْ مِنْهُ وَقَالُوا مَا أَحَدٌمِنَّا يَدْخُلُ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma ashārū kulluhum ilā Nūr al-Dīn bi-ʿayni al-ishārati iftaṣil minhu wa-qālū mā aḥadun minnā yadkhulu baynaka wa-baynahu
sentences.l: Then they signalled, all of them, to Nūr al-Dīn with the eye of the signal: Take-your-satisfaction from him! And they said: Not one of us will enter between you and him.
sentences.i: Then, one and all, they signalled to Nūr al-Dīn with a pointed glance: "Take your satisfaction of him!" And they said, "Not one of us will come between you and him."
sentences.n: The print divides the words wrongly: اشار واكلهم stands for أشاروا كلهم, “they all signalled”, the plural alif having slipped to the next word. The letters are left as printed and pointed to be read أَشَارُوا كُلُّهُمْ, the stray alif carrying no vowel. الي is the ى of إلى written with a dotted ya. افتصل منه (“settle it with him”, “take your due of him”) is a colloquial-sounding imperative whose root is not quite certain; the sense is clear. ما احدمنا is أحد منا run together.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَٰلِكَ تَقَدَّمَ نُورُ الدِّينِ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ ابْنِ سَاوِى وَكَانَ نُورُ الدِّينِ شُجَاعًا وَجَذَبَ الْوَزِيرَ مِنْ فَوْقِ سَرْجِهِ وَرَمَاهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika taqaddama Nūr al-Dīn ilā al-wazīri ibni Sāwī wa-kāna Nūr al-Dīn shujāʿan wa-jadhaba al-wazīra min fawqi sarjihi wa-ramāhu ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And at that, Nūr al-Dīn advanced to the vizier, son of Sāwī — and Nūr al-Dīn was brave — and he pulled the vizier from above his saddle and threw him on the earth.
sentences.i: Then Nūr al-Dīn stepped up to the vizier ibn Sāwī, for Nūr al-Dīn was a man of courage, and dragged him down from his saddle and hurled him to the ground.
sentences.n: وكان نور الدين شجاعا is an aside explaining why he dared; the accusative شُجَاعًا is the predicate of كَانَ.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ هُنَاكَ مَعْجَنَةُ طِينٍ فَوَقَعَ الْوَزِيرُ فِي وَسْطِهَا وَجَعَلَ يَلْطِمُهُ وَيَلْكُمُهُ فَجَاءَتْ لَكْمَةٌ عَلَى أَسْنَانِهِ فَاخْتَضَبَتْ لِحْيَةُ الْوَزِيرِ بِدَمِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna hunāka maʿjanatu ṭīnin fa-waqaʿa al-wazīru fī wasṭihā wa-jaʿala yalṭimuhu wa-yalkumuhu fa-jāʾat lakmatun ʿalā asnānihi fa-ikhtaḍabat liḥyatu al-wazīri bi-damihi
sentences.l: And there was there a kneading-trough of clay, and the vizier fell in the middle of it, and he began slapping him and punching him; and a punch came upon his teeth, and the beard of the vizier was dyed with his blood.
sentences.i: Now there lay there a trough of kneaded clay, and the vizier fell into the midst of it, and Nūr al-Dīn set to slapping and punching him, until one blow struck his teeth and the vizier's beard was dyed red with his blood.
sentences.n: كان هناك معجنة طين has the masculine كَانَ before a feminine noun; this is permitted when the verb precedes its subject. معجنة is a kneading-trough, here a heap or pit of wet clay. يلطمه is “slaps him” and يلكمه “punches him”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ مَعَ الْوَزِيرِ عَشَرَةُ مَمَالِيكَ فَلَمَّا رَأَوْا سَيِّدَهُمْ فُعِلَ بِهِ هَٰذِهِ الْفِعَالُ وَضَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ عَلَى مَقَابِضِ سُيُوفِهِمْ وَأَرَادُوا أَنْ يُجَرِّدُوهَا وَيَهْجُمُوا عَلَى نُورِ الدِّينِ عَلِيٍّ لِيَقْطَعُوهُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna maʿa al-wazīri ʿasharatu mamālīka fa-lammā raʾaw sayyidahum fuʿila bihi hādhihi al-fiʿālu waḍaʿū aydiyahum ʿalā maqābiḍi suyūfihim wa-arādū an yujarridūhā wa-yahjumū ʿalā Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī li-yaqṭaʿūhu
sentences.l: And there were with the vizier ten mamluks; and when they saw their master (that) there-had-been-done to him these deeds, they put their hands on the hilts of their swords and wanted to draw them and to rush upon Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī in-order-that-they-cut-him-down.
sentences.i: The vizier had ten mamluks with him, and when they saw what had been done to their master, they laid their hands on their sword-hilts, meaning to draw the blades and fall upon Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī and cut him down.
sentences.n: فعل به هذه الفعال is read as a passive, فُعِلَ بِهِ هَٰذِهِ الْفِعَالُ, “these deeds were done to him”; an active reading with the accusative is also possible. The printed هذه الفعال pairs a feminine demonstrative with the plural الفعال, “deeds”; the print keeps it so.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالنَّاسِ قَالُوا لِلْمَمَالِيكِ هَٰذَا وَزِيرٌ وَهَٰذَا ابْنُ وَزِيرٍ وَرُبَّمَا اصْطَلَحَا وَقْتًا آخَرَ فَتَصِيرُونَ مَبْغُوضِينَ عِنْدَ كُلٍّ مِنْهُمَا وَرُبَّمَا جَاءَتْ فِيهِ ضَرْبَةٌ فَتَمُوتُونَ جَمِيعًا أَقْبَحَ الْمَوْتَاتِ وَمِنَ الرَّأْىِ أَنْ لَا تَدْخُلُوا بَيْنَهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-nāsi qālū li-al-mamālīki hādhā wazīrun wa-hādhā ibnu wazīrin wa-rubbamā iṣṭalaḥā waqtan ākhara fa-taṣīrūna mabghūḍīna ʿinda kullin minhumā wa-rubbamā jāʾat fīhi ḍarbatun fa-tamūtūna jamīʿan aqbaḥa al-mawtāti wa-min al-raʾyi an lā tadkhulū baynahumā
sentences.l: And behold, with the people — they said to the mamluks: This (is) a vizier, and this (is) a son of a vizier; and perhaps they will make peace another time, and you will become hated with each of the two of them; and perhaps a blow will come in him, and you will die, all together, (the) ugliest of deaths; and (it is) of opinion that you not enter between the two of them.
sentences.i: Then, behold, the bystanders said to the mamluks, "This is a vizier, and that a vizier's son. They may make peace another day, and then you will be hated by both; or a blow may strike him, and then you will all die the foulest of deaths. The wise course is not to come between them."
sentences.n: وإذا بالناس: the بِـ after إِذَا marks what suddenly appears, “and behold, the people”. ربما takes a perfect here (اصطلحا, جاءت) with the sense of a future possibility, “they may make peace”. فيه in جاءت فيه ضربة is “a blow lands on him”. أقبح الموتات is an accusative of manner, “in the foulest of deaths”; ومن الرأي أن لا is “it is of good counsel that you not”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ نُورُ الدِّينِ عَلِيٌّ مِنْ ضَرْبِ الْوَزِيرِ أَخَذَ جَارِيَتَهُ وَمَضَى إِلَى دَارِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha Nūr al-Dīn ʿAliyyun min ḍarbi al-wazīri akhadha jāriyatahu wa-maḍā ilā dārihi
sentences.l: And when Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī had finished from beating the vizier, he took his slave-girl and went to his house.
sentences.i: When Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī had done with beating the vizier, he took his slave-girl and went home.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْوَزِيرُ فَمَضَى مِنْ سَاعَتِهِ وَبَقِيَ قُمَاشُهُ ثَلَٰثَةَ أَلْوَانٍ طِينٌ أَسْوَدُ وَدَمٌ أَحْمَرُ وَرَمَادٌ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-wazīru fa-maḍā min sāʿatihi wa-baqiya qumāshuhu thalāthata alwānin ṭīnun aswadu wa-damun aḥmaru wa-ramādun
sentences.l: And as for the vizier, he went from his hour; and his clothing remained three colours: clay, black; and blood, red; and ash.
sentences.i: As for the vizier, he left at once, his clothes left in three colours: black mud, red blood, and ashes.
sentences.n: The print has ثلثة without the alif of ثلاثة, marked here with the dagger alif; the three colours, listed in apposition, are the mud, the blood and the dust of the street. من ساعته, “from his hour”, means “at once”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى نَفْسَهُ عَلَى هَٰذِهِ الْحَالَةِ أَخَذَ بَرْشًا وَجَعَلَهُ فِي رَقَبَتِهِ وَأَخَذَ فِي يَدِهِ عَقْلَ تِينٍ مِنْ خَلْفِهِ سَارَ إِلَى أَنْ وَقَفَ تَحْتَ الْقَصْرِ الَّذِي فِيهِ السُّلْطَانُ وَصَاحَ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ مَظْلُومٌ مَظْلُومٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā nafsahu ʿalā hādhihi al-ḥālati akhadha barshan wa-jaʿalahu fī raqabatihi wa-akhadha fī yadihi ʿaqla tīnin min khalfihi sāra ilā an waqafa taḥta al-qaṣri al-ladhī fīhi al-sulṭānu wa-ṣāḥa yā malika al-zamāni maẓlūmun maẓlūmun
sentences.l: And when he saw himself upon this state, he took a mat and put it on his neck, and took in his hand a tying of figs (?), from behind him he went until he stood beneath the palace which in-it (was) the sultan, and cried: O king of the age, wronged, wronged!
sentences.i: Seeing the state he was in, he took a rough mat and hung it about his neck, and took a pair of cords in his hand, and so, with them trailing behind him, he walked until he stood beneath the palace where the sultan sat, and cried, "O king of the age, I am wronged, wronged!"
sentences.n: Two obscure spots. برشا is taken as a coarse mat (from برش) hung about the neck as a suppliant's sign of wretchedness. عقل تين is two words in the print; the most likely reading is a split of عقلتين, “two cords” or “two hobbles”, and the translation follows that sense, but the vowels given are those of the words as printed, and the passage may be corrupt. مظلوم مظلوم is the plaintiff's cry, “I am wronged”.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرُوهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ فَتَأَمَّلَهُ وَإِذَا بِهِ الْوَزِيرُ الْكَبِيرُ فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَزِيرُ مَنْ فَعَلَ بِكَ هَٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍarūhu bayna yadayhi fa-taʾammalahu wa-idhā bihi al-wazīru al-kabīru fa-qāla lahu yā wazīru man faʿala bika hādhihi al-fiʿāla
sentences.l: So they brought him between his two hands; and he scrutinised him, and behold, with him (it was) the vizier, the great; and he said to him: O vizier, who did to you these deeds?
sentences.i: They brought him before the sultan, who looked at him closely and saw, behold, his chief vizier. "Vizier," he said, "who has done this to you?"
sentences.n: وإذا به الوزير الكبير: again بِـ after إِذَا of surprise, “and behold, it was the chief vizier”. The sultan is the subject of تأمله and قال.

sentences.t: فَبَكَى وَانْتَحَبَ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-bakā wa-intaḥaba wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And he wept and sobbed and recited, saying, verse:
sentences.i: He wept and sobbed aloud, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print has the single word شعر, the rubric that introduces a poem; it is read as a bare label, شِعْرٌ.

sentences.t:
اَيَظْلِمُنِى الزَّمَانُ وَاَنْتَ فِيهِ * وَتَأْكُلُنِى الذِّيَابُ وَاَنْتَ لَيْثُ
وَيُرْوَى مِنْ حِيَاضِكَ كُلُّ ظَامٍ * وَأَظْمَأُ فِي حِمَاكَ وَاَنْتَ غَيْثُ
sentences.tr:
a-yaẓlimunī al-zamānu wa-anta fīhi * wa-taʾkulunī al-dhiyābu wa-anta laythun
wa-yurwā min ḥiyāḍika kullu ẓāmin * wa-aẓmaʾu fī ḥimāka wa-anta ghaythun
sentences.l:
Will Time wrong me, while you are in it, * and will the wolves eat me, while you are a lion?
And every thirsty one is watered from your cisterns, * and I thirst in your protection, while you are rain?
sentences.i:
Shall Time wrong me while you live in it, * and wolves devour me while you are a lion?
From your pools every thirsty soul is watered, * yet I go dry under your protection, when you are the rain!
sentences.n: Verse, copied exactly as pointed in the print. الذياب is the print's spelling of الذئاب, “the wolves”, with ya for the hamza. The vizier reproaches his sovereign: he is wronged and devoured under a king who ought to be both lion and rain-cloud for his subjects.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ يَا سَيِّدِي كُلُّ مَنْ كَانَ يُحِبُّكَ وَيَخْدُمُكَ يَجْرِي عَلَيْهِ هَٰكَذَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla yā sayyidī kullu man kāna yuḥibbuka wa-yakhdumuka yajrī ʿalayhi hākadhā
sentences.l: Then he said: O my lord, everyone who was loving you and serving you, it runs upon him thus.
sentences.i: Then he said, "My lord, everyone who loves and serves you ends up like this."

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ السُّلْطَانُ وَلَكَ عَجِّلْ وَقُلْ لِي كَيْفَ جَرَى لَكَ هَذَا وَمَنْ فَعَلَ بِكَ هَذِهِ الْفِعَالَ وَأَنْتَ حُرْمَتُكَ مِنْ حُرْمَتِي
sentences.tr: qāla lahu al-sulṭānu wa-laka ʿajjil wa-qul lī kayfa jarā laka hādhā wa-man faʿala bika hādhihi al-fiʿāla wa-anta ḥurmatuka min ḥurmatī
sentences.l: Said to-him the sultan: And-to-you — hurry, and say to me how it ran for you, this, and who did with you these deeds, and you, your inviolability is from my inviolability.
sentences.i: The sultan said to him: "Come, man, be quick, and tell me how this befell you and who has done such deeds to you — you, whose person is as sacred as my own!"
sentences.n: The sultan has just seen his vizier battered and bleeding. وَلَكَ (wa-laka, literally “and to you”) is a brusque colloquial summons, something like “hey, you” or “look here”, and is not Classical. The last clause is a bare nominal sentence: “you — your sanctity is from my sanctity”, meaning an insult to the vizier is an insult to the sultan.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ اعْلَمْ يَا سَيِّدِي أَنِّي خَرَجْتُ الْيَوْمَ إِلَى سُوقِ الْجَوَارِي عَلَى أَنِّي أَشْتَرِي جَارِيَةً طَبَّاخَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru iʿlam yā sayyidī annī kharajtu al-yawma ilā sūqi al-jawārī ʿalā annī ashtarī jāriyatan ṭabbākhatan
sentences.l: And said the vizier: Know, O my master, that I went-out today to the market of the slave-girls, on that I buy a slave-girl, a cook.
sentences.i: The vizier said: "Know, my lord, that I went out today to the slave-market, intending to buy a girl who could cook."
sentences.n: عَلَى أَنِّي أَشْتَرِي is “with the intention that I buy”; the verb is a bare indicative, where Classical would more often use a subjunctive after أن. The same bare indicative recurs below (أَرَدْتُ أَشْتَرِيهَا).

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ فِى السُّوقِ جَارِيَةً مَا رَأَيْتُ أَحْسَنَ طُولَ عُمْرِي مِثْلَهَا فَأَرَدْتُ أَشْتَرِيهَا لِمَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانِ فَسَأَلْتُ عَنْهَا الدَّلَّالَ وَعَنْ سَيِّدِهَا فَقَالَ الدَّلَّالُ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu fī al-sūqi jāriyatan mā raʾaytu aḥsana ṭūla ʿumrī mithlahā fa-aradtu ashtarīhā li-mawlānā al-sulṭāni fa-saʾaltu ʿanhā al-dallāla wa-ʿan sayyidihā fa-qāla al-dallālu
sentences.l: So I saw in the market a slave-girl, not did I see, more beautiful (in) the length of my life, her like; so I wished I buy-her for our master the sultan; so I asked about-her the broker and about her master; so said the broker:
sentences.i: In the market I saw a girl the like of whom, for beauty, I have not seen in all my long life, and I wished to buy her for our lord the sultan. So I asked the broker about her, and about her owner, and the broker said:
sentences.n: The relative clause has no linking word and ends with مِثْلَهَا, “her like”. Note again the bare indicative أَرَدْتُ أَشْتَرِيهَا, “I wished I buy her”, with no أن. فِى is printed with ى, so it is kept as written. أَحْسَنَ is accusative as the object of the “seeing”, with طُولَ عُمْرِي an adverbial accusative: “for the length of my life”.

sentences.t: إِنَّهَا لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ الْفَضْلِ بْنِ خَاقَانَ وَكَانَ مَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانُ أَعْطَى سَابِقًا لِأَبِيهِ عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ لِيَشْتَرِيَ بِهَا جَارِيَةً مَلِيحَةً فَاشْتَرَى تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةَ فَأَعْجَبَتْهُ فَبَخِلَ بِهَا عَلَى مَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانِ فَأَعْطَاهَا لِوَلَدِهِ
sentences.tr: innahā li-ʿAlī ibn al-Faḍl ibn Khāqān wa-kāna mawlānā al-sulṭānu aʿṭā sābiqan li-abīhi ʿasharata ālāfi dīnārin li-yashtariya bihā jāriyatan malīḥatan fa-ishtarā tilka al-jāriyata fa-aʿjabathu fa-bakhila bihā ʿalā mawlānā al-sulṭāni fa-aʿṭāhā li-waladihi
sentences.l: "Indeed-she (is) to ʿAlī, son of al-Faḍl, son of Khāqān; and our master the sultan had given, formerly, to his father ten thousands (of) dinar, that he buy with-them a slave-girl, a pretty one; so he bought that slave-girl, so she pleased-him, so he was-stingy with-her toward our master the sultan, so he gave-her to his son.
sentences.i: "She belongs to ʿAlī ibn al-Faḍl ibn Khāqān. Our lord the sultan once gave his father ten thousand dinars to buy a pretty girl; he bought this one, and she pleased him so well that he grudged her to our lord the sultan and gave her to his own son."
sentences.n: The broker's words are still being reported by the vizier. لِيَشْتَرِيَ بِهَا, “that he buy with it”, takes the money as the instrument. بَخِلَ بِهَا عَلَى, “be stingy with her toward”, uses بِـ for what is withheld and عَلَى for the person denied.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا مَاتَ أَبُوهُ بَاعَ ابْنُهُ جَمِيعَ مَا عِنْدَهُ مِنَ الْأَ مْلَاكِ وَالْبَسَاتِينِ وَالْأَ وَانِي حَتَّى أَفْلَسَ فَنَزَلَ بِالْجَارِيَةِ إِلَى السُّوقِ عَلَى أَنْ يَبِيعَهَا وَسَلَّمَهَا لِلدَّلَّالِ فَنَادَى عَلَيْهَا وَتَزَايَدَتِ النُّجَّارُ فِيهَا حَتَّى وَصَلَتْ ثَمَنُهَا أَرْبَعَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā māta abūhu bāʿa ibnuhu jamīʿa mā ʿindahu min al-amlāki wa-al-basātīni wa-al-awānī ḥattā aflasa fa-nazala bi-al-jāriyati ilā al-sūqi ʿalā an yabīʿahā wa-sallamahā li-al-dallāli fa-nādā ʿalayhā wa-tazāyadati al-nujjāru fīhā ḥattā waṣalat thamanuhā arbaʿata ālāfi dīnārin
sentences.l: So when died his father, sold his son the whole of what (was) with him of the properties and the gardens and the vessels, until he went-bankrupt; so he went-down with the slave-girl to the market, on that he sell-her, and handed-her to the broker; so he cried (the sale) over her, and increased the …-ers in her, until reached her price four thousands (of) dinar.
sentences.i: When his father died, the son sold everything he owned — lands, gardens and household goods — until he was ruined. Then he brought the girl down to the market to sell her and handed her to the broker, who cried her for sale; the bidders pressed her price higher and higher until it reached four thousand dinars.
sentences.n: The edition prints الا ملاك and والا واني with a space after the alif, so the words are broken in the print; they are الأملاك, “properties”, and الأواني, “vessels”, and are pointed here as printed, split where the print splits. النجار as printed is النُّجَّار, “the carpenters”; the sense plainly wants التُّجَّار, “the merchants” (the bidders), so the nūn is probably a compositor's slip for tāʾ, but the letter is kept. The feminine verb تَزَايَدَتِ before the plural النُّجَّار, and وَصَلَتْ ثَمَنُهَا with the price as grammatical subject, are both loose usage; the vocalisation follows what is printed.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لِعَقْلِي أَشْتَرِي هَذِهِ لِمَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانِ فَإِنَّ ثَمَنَهَا فِى الْأَصْلِ كَانَ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu li-ʿaqlī ashtarī hādhihi li-mawlānā al-sulṭāni fa-inna thamanahā fī al-aṣli kāna min ʿindihi
sentences.l: So I said to my mind: I buy this one for our master the sultan, for indeed her price in the origin was from with-him.
sentences.i: I said to myself: "I will buy this one for our lord the sultan, for her price came in the beginning from him."
sentences.n: قُلْتُ لِعَقْلِي, “I said to my mind”, is the idiom for talking to oneself. مِنْ عِنْدِهِ, “from with him”, means the money was originally the sultan's own gift.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ يَا وَلَدِي خُذْ ثَمَنَهَا مِنِّي أَرْبَعَةَ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu yā waladī khudh thamanahā minnī arbaʿata ālāfi dīnārin
sentences.l: So I said: O my son, take her price from me, four thousands (of) dinar.
sentences.i: So I said: "My son, take her price from me: four thousand dinars."

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامِي نَظَرَ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ يَا شَيْخَ النَّحْسِ أَنَا أَبِيعُهَا لِلْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَلَا أَبِيعُهَا لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmī naẓara ilayya wa-qāla yā shaykha al-naḥsi anā abīʿuhā li-al-yahūdi wa-al-naṣārā wa-lā abīʿuhā laka
sentences.l: So when he heard my speech, he looked at me and said: O old-man of the ill-luck, I — I sell-her to the Jews and the Christians, and not do I sell-her to you.
sentences.i: When he heard me, he stared at me and said: "You ill-omened old man! I would sell her to Jews and Christians before I would sell her to you!"
sentences.n: شَيْخَ النَّحْسِ is “old man of ill luck”, a harsh insult; the vocative is in construct, so شَيْخَ takes the accusative. The sentence is a flat denial in the present tense (“I sell her to the Jews … and I do not sell her to you”) and is meant as defiance.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ أَنَا مَا أَشْتَرِيهَا لِنَفْسِي وَإِنَّمَا أَشْتَرِيهَا لِمَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانِ الَّذِي هُوَ وَلِيُّ نِعْمَتِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qultu anā mā ashtarīhā li-nafsī wa-innamā ashtarīhā li-mawlānā al-sulṭāni alladhī huwa waliyyu niʿmatinā
sentences.l: So I said: I, not do I buy-her for myself, and only I buy-her for our master the sultan, who he (is) the patron of our favour.
sentences.i: I said: "I am not buying her for myself; I am buying her only for our lord the sultan, who is our benefactor."
sentences.n: وَلِيُّ نِعْمَتِنَا, “the patron of our bounty”, is the stock courtly phrase for the one to whom a subject owes his livelihood.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنِّي هَذَا الْكَلَامَ اغْتَاظَ وَجَذَبَنِي وَرَمَانِي عَنِ الْجَوَادِ وَأَنَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ وَضَرَبَنِي بِيَدِهِ وَلَكَمَنِي حَتَّى تَرَكَنِي كَمَا تَرَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa minnī hādhā al-kalāma ightāẓa wa-jadhabanī wa-ramānī ʿani al-jawādi wa-anā shaykhun kabīrun wa-ḍarabanī bi-yadihi wa-lakamanī ḥattā tarakanī ka-mā tarānī
sentences.l: So when he heard from me this speech, he was-enraged, and pulled me, and threw me from the horse, and I (am) an old man, great (in years), and struck me with his hand, and punched me until he left me as you see me.
sentences.i: When he heard these words from me he flew into a rage, dragged me down and flung me off my horse — and I an old man of great age — then struck me with his hand and punched me until he left me as you see me now.
sentences.n: جَوَاد is the “fine horse”, here simply the vizier's mount. The circumstantial clause وَأَنَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ, “and I an old man”, is the vizier's plea for pity. The ka- of كَمَا تَرَانِي is “like”: “as you see me”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا مَا أَوْقَعَنِي فِي هَذَا كُلِّهِ إِلَّا أَنِّي جِئْتُ أَشْتَرِي هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ لَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā mā awqaʿanī fī hādhā kullihi illā annī jiʾtu ashtarī hādhihi al-jāriyata laka
sentences.l: And I, nothing made-me-fall into this, all of it, except that I came (to) buy this slave-girl for you.
sentences.i: "And nothing has brought all this upon me, but that I came to buy this girl for you."
sentences.n: The “nothing … except” construction (مَا … إِلَّا) is the standard way to say “only because”. جِئْتُ أَشْتَرِي, “I came I buy”, again puts the second verb in the bare indicative.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْوَزِيرَ أَرْمَى نَفْسَهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ وَجَعَلَ يَبْكِي وَيَرْتَعِدُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-wazīra armā nafsahu ʿalā al-arḍi wa-jaʿala yabkī wa-yartaʿidu
sentences.l: Then indeed the vizier cast his self on the earth, and began weeping and trembling.
sentences.i: Then the vizier threw himself on the ground and began to weep and tremble.
sentences.n: أَرْمَى is the form IV of رمى; Classical would say رَمَى نَفْسَهُ or أَلْقَى نَفْسَهُ. The print writes it ارمى, and it is pointed as the print has it. جَعَلَ يَبْكِي, “he made/set to weeping”, is the regular way to say “began to weep”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ السُّلْطَانُ إِلَى حَالَتِهِ وَسَمِعَ مَقَالَتَهُ قَامَ عِرْقُ الْغَضَبِ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara al-sulṭānu ilā ḥālatihi wa-samiʿa maqālatahu qāma ʿirqu al-ghaḍabi bayna ʿaynayhi
sentences.l: So when the sultan looked at his state and heard his saying, rose the vein of the anger between his two eyes.
sentences.i: When the sultan saw his state and heard his tale, the vein of anger stood out between his eyes.
sentences.n: عِرْقُ الْغَضَبِ, “the vein of anger”, is the swelling vein on the forehead.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى أَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَإِذَا بِأَرْبَعِينَ رَجُلٍ ضَارِبِينَ سُيُوفًا وَقَفُوا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā arbābi al-dawlati wa-idhā bi-arbaʿīna rajulin ḍāribīna suyūfan waqafū bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: Then he turned to the lords of the state, and behold, with forty man, strikers (of) swords, they stood between his two hands.
sentences.i: Then he turned to the lords of the state — and there stood before him forty men with drawn swords.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِ… is “and behold …”; the بِـ after إِذَا of surprise only marks what appears. The numeral takes a singular noun, here with the genitive رَجُلٍ as the print allows. ضَارِبِينَ سُيُوفًا, “strikers of swords”, is a loose circumstantial phrase for men armed with swords; the participle is pointed as an accusative state-word agreeing with the forty. بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ, “between his hands”, means “in his presence”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمُ السُّلْطَانُ انْزِلُوا السَّاعَةَ إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ خَاقَانَ وَانْهَبُوهَا وَاهْدِمُوهَا وَائْتُونِي بِهِ وَبِالْجَارِيَةِ مُكَتَّفِينَ وَاسْحَبُوهُمَا عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمَا وَأْتُوابِهِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahumu al-sulṭānu inzilū al-sāʿata ilā dāri ʿAlī ibn Khāqān wa-inhabūhā wa-ihdimūhā wa-ʾtūnī bihi wa-bi-al-jāriyati mukattafīna wa-isḥabūhumā ʿalā wujūhihimā wa-ʾtū bihimā bayna yadayya
sentences.l: So said to-them the sultan: Go-down this hour to the house of ʿAlī, son of Khāqān, and plunder-it, and demolish-it, and bring-me him and the slave-girl, bound-ones, and drag-them on their faces, and bring them between my hands.
sentences.i: The sultan said to them: "Go down at once to the house of ʿAlī ibn Khāqān; plunder it and raze it, and bring me him and the girl bound hand and foot. Drag them here on their faces and set them before me!"
sentences.n: أَتَى بِـ means “bring”, with the thing brought taking بِـ: وَائْتُونِي بِهِ, “bring me him”. The last verb is printed واتوابهما with the verb and its pronoun joined, and is pointed as one written word. مُكَتَّفِينَ is “bound”, with the arms tied.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَهُ السَّمْعُ وَالطَّاعَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lahu al-samʿu wa-al-ṭāʿatu
sentences.l: So they said to-him: The hearing and the obedience.
sentences.i: They answered him with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: السمع والطاعة is the courtly formula of acceptance, a nominal phrase with the verb understood: “(ours is) hearing and obedience”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ لَبِسُوا الْعُدَدَ وَنَزَلُوا وَعَوَّلُو عَلَى الْمَسِيرِ إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيٍّ نُورِالدِّينِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum labisū al-ʿudada wa-nazalū wa-ʿawwalū ʿalā al-masīri ilā dāri ʿAlī Nūri al-Dīn
sentences.l: Then indeed they put-on the equipment, and went-down, and relied on the going to the house of ʿAlī Nūr al-Dīn.
sentences.i: Then they put on their gear, went down, and set out for the house of ʿAlī Nūr al-Dīn.
sentences.n: The print writes عولو without the final alif of the plural ending, so the verb عَوَّلُوا (ʿawwala ʿalā, “to resolve upon”) is pointed on the printed letters, with no alif. Nūr al-Dīn is printed as one word, نورالدين, and is pointed as one.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ عِنْدَ السُّلْطَانِ حَاجِبٌ يُقَالُ لَهُ عَلَمُ الدِّينِ سَنْجَرُ وَكَانَ أَوَّلًا مِنْ مَمَالِيكِ الْفَضْلِ بْنِ خَاقَانَ وَآلِ عَلِيٍّ نُورِالدِّينِ ثُمَّ انْتَقَلَتْ مَنْزِلَتُهُ إِلَى أَنْ عَمَّلَهُ السُّلْطَانُ حَاجِبًا عِنْدَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ʿinda al-sulṭāni ḥājibun yuqālu lahu ʿAlamu al-Dīni Sanjaru wa-kāna awwalan min mamālīki al-Faḍli ibn Khāqān wa-āli ʿAlī Nūri al-Dīn thumma intaqalat manzilatuhu ilā an ʿammalahu al-sulṭānu ḥājiban ʿindahu
sentences.l: And there was with the sultan a chamberlain, it is said to him ʿAlam al-Dīn Sanjar; and he was at first among the slaves of al-Faḍl, son of Khāqān, and the family of ʿAlī Nūr al-Dīn; then his rank moved, until the sultan made-him-an-official, a chamberlain, with him.
sentences.i: Now the sultan had a chamberlain called ʿAlam al-Dīn Sanjar, who had begun as one of the mamluks of al-Faḍl ibn Khāqān and the household of ʿAlī Nūr al-Dīn; then his fortunes rose, until the sultan made him his own chamberlain.
sentences.n: The print has وال علي نورالدين with the alif of آل unmarked, and it is pointed here as وَآلِ, “and the family of”. عَمَّلَهُ is read as form II of عمل, “to appoint someone as an officer”, with حَاجِبًا as the second accusative.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مَرْسُومَ السُّلْطَانِ وَرَأَى الْأَعْدَاءَ تَجَهَّزُوا إِلَى قَتْلِ ابْنِ سَيِّدِهِ مَاهَانَ عَلَيْهِ فَغَابَ مِنْ قُدَّامِ السُّلْطَانِ وَرَكِبَ جَوَادَهُ وَسَارَ إِلَى أَنْ جَاءَ إِلَى بَيْتِ نُورِالدِّينِ عَلِيٍّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa marsūma al-sulṭāni wa-raʾā al-aʿdāʾa tajahhazū ilā qatli ibni sayyidihi māhāna ʿalayhi fa-ghāba min quddāmi al-sulṭāni wa-rakiba jawādahu wa-sāra ilā an jāʾa ilā bayti Nūri al-Dīn ʿAlī
sentences.l: So when he heard the decree of the sultan, and saw the enemies (who) had equipped themselves for the killing of the son of his master, not-was-light on him; so he disappeared from before the sultan, and rode his horse, and went until he came to the house of Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī.
sentences.i: When he heard the sultan's decree and saw the soldiers armed to kill his master's son, he could not bear it; he slipped away from the sultan's presence, mounted his horse, and rode until he came to the house of Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī.
sentences.n: ماهان is printed as one word and is read as مَا هَانَ عَلَيْهِ, “it was not light upon him”, meaning he could not bear it; it is the only reading that fits, though the print leaves the two words joined. الأعداء, “the enemies”, is the chamberlain's own word for the soldiers who go to kill his old master's son; تَجَهَّزُوا is a circumstantial clause with no linking word. قُدَّام is the common “in front of / presence”.

sentences.t: فَطَرَقَ الْبَابَ فَخَرَجَ لَهُ نُورُالدِّينِ فَلَمَّا رَآهُ عَرَفَهُ فَقَالَ يَاسَيِّدِي مَا هَذَا وَقْتُ سَلَامٍ وَلَا كَلَامٍ وَاسْمَعْ مَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭaraqa al-bāba fa-kharaja lahu Nūru al-Dīni fa-lammā raʾāhu ʿarafahu fa-qāla yā-sayyidī mā hādhā waqtu salāmin wa-lā kalāmin wa-ismaʿ mā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: So he knocked the door, so came-out to him Nūr al-Dīn; so when he saw him, he knew him; so he said: O my master, not this (is) a time of greeting and not of talk; and hear what the poet said:
sentences.i: He knocked at the door, and Nūr al-Dīn came out to him, and, seeing him, knew him. Sanjar said: "My lord, this is no time for greetings or for talk. Hear what the poet said:"
sentences.n: The print joins يا and سيدي into ياسيدي; it is pointed as one word. Here رَآهُ keeps the precomposed آ, as the edition prints it.

sentences.t:
وَنَفْسَكَ فُزْبِهَا اِنْ صِبْتَ ضَيْمًا * وَخَلِّ الدَّارَ تَنْعَى مَنْ بَنَا هَا
فَاِنَّكَ وَاجِدُ اَرْضًا بِاَرْضِ * وَنَفْسَكَ لَمْ تَجِدْ نَفْسًا سِوَا هَا
sentences.tr:
wa-nafsaka fuz bihā in ṣibta ḍaymān * wa-khalli al-dāra tanʿā man banā hā
fa-innaka wājidu arḍan bi-arḍi * wa-nafsaka lam tajid nafsan siwā hā
sentences.l: And your self — win-through with-it, if you are-struck (by) injustice; and leave the house, it mourns whoever built it. For indeed-you (are) finder of a land for a land, and your self — not will you find a self other-than-it.
sentences.i: Save your own self, if wrong should strike you, and leave the house to mourn the one who built it. You will find land to take the place of land, but never another self to take the place of your own.
sentences.n: These two lines are printed with full pointing, which is copied here exactly; the print also separates the pronoun in بَنَا هَا and سِوَا هَا and joins the verb and preposition in فُزْبِهَا. Reading: فُزْ بِهَا, “win through with it”, from فاز بِـ; the verb ضام (ضَيْمًا, “wrong, injustice”) with صِبْتَ is the printed form. In the second hemistich of the first line تَنْعَى is read as “mourns”, the house being imagined as lamenting its builder; the commonest sense of the line is “abandon the house — let it grieve for the man who built it”. The print gives وَاجِدُ with a damma and no tanwīn, which is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ نُورُالدِّينِ يَا عَلَمَ الدِّينِ مَا الْخَبَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Nūru al-Dīni yā ʿAlama al-Dīni mā al-khabaru
sentences.l: So said Nūr al-Dīn: O ʿAlam al-Dīn, what the news?
sentences.i: Nūr al-Dīn said: "ʿAlam al-Dīn, what is the news?"

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ انْهَضْ وَفُزْ بِنَفْسِكَ أَنْتَ وَالْجَارِيَةُ فَإِنَّ الْمُعِينَ بْنَ سَاوَى نَصَبَ لَكُمَا شَرَكًا وَمَتَى وَقَعْتُمَا فِي يَدِهِ قَتَلَكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu inhaḍ wa-fuz bi-nafsika anta wa-al-jāriyatu fa-inna al-Muʿīna ibna Sāwā naṣaba lakumā sharakan wa-matā waqaʿtumā fī yadihi qatalakumā
sentences.l: So he said to-him: Rise, and win-through with your self, you and the slave-girl; for indeed al-Muʿīn, son of Sāwī, has-set for-you-two a snare, and whenever you-two fall in his hand, he kills-you-two.
sentences.i: He said: "Rise, and save yourself, you and the girl, for al-Muʿīn ibn Sāwī has set a snare for you both, and if you fall into his hand he will kill you."
sentences.n: أَنْتَ وَالْجَارِيَةُ is the pronoun “you” stressing the implied subject of فُزْ, with the girl joined on in the nominative. مَتَى here means “if ever / whenever” and takes the perfect.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَيَّرَ لَكُمَا السُّلْطَانُ أَرْبَعِينَ ضَارِبًا بِالسَّيْفِ وَالرَّأْيُ عِنْدِي أَنْ تَهْرُبَا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَحِلَّ الضَّرَرُ بِكُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad sayyara lakumā al-sulṭānu arbaʿīna ḍāriban bi-al-sayfi wa-al-raʾyu ʿindī an tahrubā qabla an yaḥilla al-ḍararu bikumā
sentences.l: And already has-sent for-you-two the sultan forty strikers with the sword; and the opinion (is) with me that you-two flee before that descends the harm on-you-two.
sentences.i: "The sultan has already sent forty swordsmen after you, and my counsel is that you flee before the harm comes down on you."
sentences.n: الرأي عندي, “the opinion is with me”, means “my advice is”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ سَنْجَرَ مَدَّيَدَهُ إِلَى صُولَتِهِ فَوَجَدَ فِيهِ أَرْبَعِينَ دِينَارًا فَأَخَذَهُمْ وَأَعْطَاهُمْ إِلَى نُورِ الدِّينِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Sanjara maddayadahu ilā ṣūlatihi fa-wajada fīhi arbaʿīna dīnāran fa-akhadhahum wa-aʿṭāhum ilā Nūri al-Dīn
sentences.l: Then indeed Sanjar stretched his hand to his … , so he found in it forty dinar, so he took them and gave them to Nūr al-Dīn.
sentences.i: Then Sanjar put his hand into his purse and found in it forty dinars; he took them out and gave them to Nūr al-Dīn.
sentences.n: The print has مديده, which is مَدَّ يَدَهُ with the two words joined, “he stretched his hand”. صولته as printed would be “his assault”, which cannot be right for something he finds money in; the sense calls for صُرَّتِهِ, “his purse”, so it is probably a printer's slip, but the letters are kept and pointed as printed. The pronoun in فِيهِ refers to it and the coins are then plural, أَخَذَهُمْ, as the print has it.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي خُذْ هَذِهِ وَسَافِرْ بِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ مَعِي أَكْثَرُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ لَأَعْطَيْتُكَ إِيَّاهُ لَكِنْ مَا هَذَا وَقْتُ مُعَاتَبَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā-sayyidī khudh hādhihi wa-sāfir bihim wa-law kāna maʿī aktharu min dhālika la-aʿṭaytuka iyyāhu lākin mā hādhā waqtu muʿātabatin
sentences.l: And he said to-him: O my master, take this, and travel with-them; and if there were with me more than that, I would have given-you it; but not this (is) a time of reproach.
sentences.i: He said: "My lord, take these and travel with them. Had I more than this, I would give it to you, but this is no time for lamenting."
sentences.n: سَافِرْ بِهِمْ is “travel with them”, the coins treated as plural persons. مُعَاتَبَة is “reproach, mutual blame”; the sense is that there is no time for apology that the sum is small.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ دَخَلَ نُورُ الدِّينِ عَلَى الْجَارِيَةِ وَأَعْلَمَهَا بِذَلِكَ فَتَخَبَّلَتْ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika dakhala Nūru al-Dīni ʿalā al-jāriyati wa-aʿlamahā bi-dhālika fa-takhabbalat yadayhā
sentences.l: So at that, entered Nūr al-Dīn on the slave-girl and informed-her of that; so she became-crippled (as to) her two hands.
sentences.i: At that Nūr al-Dīn went in to the girl and told her; and she was struck numb, her hands failing her.
sentences.n: The form فتخبلت يديها is obscure. It reads as the fifth form of خبل, “to be crippled, bewildered”, with يَدَيْهَا as an accusative of respect: “she was stricken in her hands”. The meaning of the whole is surely that she was struck helpless with shock, but this is an inference, and the word may be corrupt (possibly a verb meaning “she clasped/wrung” her hands). دَخَلَ عَلَى is the ordinary “go in to” a person's presence.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ الِاثْنَانِ فِي الْوَقْتِ أَىْ ظَاهِرِ الْمَدِينَةِ.
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja al-ithnāni fī al-waqti ay ẓāhiri al-madīnati
sentences.l: Then went-out the two in the time, that is the outside (of) the city.
sentences.i: Then the two of them went out immediately, to the outskirts of the city.
sentences.n: The print puts a full stop here, so the sentence ends at the city. فِي الْوَقْتِ, “in the moment”, means “at once”. أَىْ (printed اى) is “that is”, and it introduces ظَاهِرِ الْمَدِينَةِ, “the outside of the city”, as an explanation of فِي الْوَقْتِ; the sentence is loose, and the genitive is pointed as the construct reads.

sentences.t: وَأَسْبَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمَا سِتْرَهُ وَمَشَيَا إِلَى سَاحِلِ الْبَحْرِ فَوَجَدَا مَرْكَبًا تَجَهَّزَتْ لِلْمَسْفَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-asbala Allāhu ʿalayhimā sitrahu wa-mashayā ilā sāḥili al-baḥri fa-wajadā markaban tajahhazat li-al-masfari
sentences.l: And God let-down upon-them-two His veil, and they-two walked to the shore of the sea, and found a ship (which) had-been-made-ready for the voyage.
sentences.i: God drew His veil over them, and they walked to the seashore, where they found a ship made ready for a voyage.
sentences.n: أَسْبَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمَا سِتْرَهُ, “God let down His veil over them”, is the stock phrase for divine protection that hides a person. The ship is masculine but the verb is feminine, تَجَهَّزَتْ; the print gives it so.

sentences.t: وَالرَّئِيسُ وَاقِفٌ فِي وَسْطِ الْمَرْكَبِ يَقُولُ مَنْ بَقِيَ لَهُ حَاجَةٌ مِنْ زَادِهِ أَوْ مِنْ وَدَاعِ أَهْلِهِ أَوْ مَنْ نَسِيَ حَاجَةً فَلْيَأْتِ بِهَا فَإِنَّنَا مُتَوَجِّهُونَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-raʾīsu wāqifun fī wasṭi al-markabi yaqūlu man baqiya lahu ḥājatun min zādihi aw min wadāʿi ahlihi aw man nasiya ḥājatan fa-li-yaʾti bihā fa-innanā mutawajjihūna
sentences.l: And the captain (was) standing in the middle of the ship, saying: Whoever remains to-him a need from his provisions, or from the farewell (to) his family, or whoever forgot a need, then let him bring it; for indeed-we (are) heading-out.
sentences.i: The captain stood amidships crying: "Whoever still lacks anything for his journey, or has not yet taken leave of his family, or has forgotten some need, let him fetch it now, for we are about to sail!"
sentences.n: The second مَنْ is printed as the first word of a new clause and can be read as “or whoever”; the print does not repeat مِنْ before it and the vowels follow that. فَلْيَأْتِ بِهَا is “let him bring it” (أَتَى بِـ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كُلُّهُمْ لَمْ يَبْقَ لَنَا شُغْلٌ يَا رَئِيسُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla kulluhum lam yabqa lanā shughlun yā raʾīsu
sentences.l: So said all-of-them: Not remains to-us business, O captain.
sentences.i: They all answered: "We lack nothing, captain."

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ الرَّئِيسُ لِجَمَاعَتِهِ هَيَّا حُلُّوا الْأَطْرَافَ وَاقْلَعُوا الْأَوْتَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāla al-raʾīsu li-jamāʿatihi hayyā ḥullū al-aṭrāfa wa-iqlaʿū al-awtāda
sentences.l: So at that said the captain to his group: Come, loose the ends, and pull-up the pegs.
sentences.i: Then the captain said to his crew: "Come, loose the ropes and pull up the anchor-stakes!"
sentences.n: الأطراف, “the ends”, are the mooring ropes; الأوتاد, “the pegs”, are the stakes to which the ship is tied.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ نُورُالدِّينِ عَلِيٌّ إِلَى أَيْنَ يَارَئِيسُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Nūru al-Dīni ʿAliyyun ilā ayna yā-raʾīsu
sentences.l: So said Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī: To where, O captain?
sentences.i: Nūr al-Dīn ʿAlī asked: "Where to, captain?"
sentences.n: The print joins يا and رئيس into يارئيس; it is pointed as one word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ إِلَى دَارِ السَّلَامِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ilā dāri al-salāmi Baghdāda
sentences.l: So he said: To the abode of the peace, Baghdad.
sentences.i: "To the Abode of Peace," he said, "to Baghdad."

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, so she fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unfinished.
sentences.n: The formulaic close of a night. The two last words rhyme (aṣ-ṣabāḥ … al-mubāḥ), the sajʿ that ends every night; “permitted speech” is the stock phrase for what she is allowed to say.
